Research lab · Concordia University

Urban Microclimate & Built Environment

We study urban microclimate: how buildings, streets and vegetation shape local heat, airflow and air quality, and how those conditions affect indoor comfort, energy use and health. We combine field measurements, physics-based simulation and AI to help communities adapt to a changing climate.

NEURIPS 2026 SPOTLIGHT

GeoWind2Plan

Fast, building-resolved wind predictions help compare the energy use of simulated drone routes. This collaboration shows one application of urban microclimate modelling: using local airflow to inform a planning decision.

Liangzhu Leon Wang is a co-corresponding author.

Lab lead

Liangzhu Leon Wang

Professor of Building, Civil and Environmental Engineering and Associate Director of the Centre for Zero Energy Building Studies, Concordia University

Concordia faculty profile

Current research

Wang leads UMBE-LAB, where he studies how urban microclimate and buildings influence each other. His team examines how neighbourhood conditions affect indoor overheating, ventilation, energy demand and human exposure. It combines laboratory experiments, field monitoring, physics-based simulation and AI to develop digital twins of buildings and neighbourhoods.

He leads Volt-Age’s Transforming Built and Urban Microclimates project, which measures heat exposure and tests ways to protect vulnerable communities as buildings electrify.

His Canadian research collaborators include the National Research Council Canada, Environment and Climate Change Canada, Health Canada, the Standards Council of Canada, and Natural Resources Canada.

Earlier work and engineering impact

Working with the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, Wang helped develop multizone building airflow models and methods to predict the movement of contaminants and smoke. His research on carbon monoxide from portable emergency gasoline generators informed guidance from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and rulemaking by the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission.

His research also contributed to the International Energy Conservation Code, ASHRAE Standards 90.1 and 189.1, California’s Building Energy Efficiency Standards (Title 24), and ANSI/AMCA Standard 220. In Canada, his work informed ventilation guidance during COVID-19, building overheating assessments, and national recommendations for mapping extreme heat.

Research

From rooms to cities

01 · Microclimate

Urban form and local climate

We study how buildings, streets and vegetation shape shade, heat, airflow and pollutant dispersion at pedestrian and neighbourhood scales.

02 · Buildings

Buildings, energy and health

We connect outdoor microclimate with indoor overheating, ventilation, air quality and energy demand to assess health risks and compare adaptation measures.

03 · Methods

Measurement, simulation and AI

We combine field monitoring, physics-based simulation and AI to resolve neighbourhood conditions, test predictions against measurements and evaluate design and retrofit options.

Tools for urban research

Simulation and datasets

CityScaLES

A scalable multi-GPU simulation engine for urban microclimate, resolving airflow and heat transfer around buildings. It builds on the lab’s CityFFD work.

DocumentationCityFFD dataset

AI emulator

FLUME

A geometry-aware urban microclimate emulator that rapidly predicts three-dimensional airflow and temperature fields.

RepositoryPreprint

Building energy

CityBEM

Urban building energy modelling for studying energy use and comparing building and retrofit scenarios.
